newsitem.title: GERMANY: Blair tells Kohl to modernise for jobs and EMU.
newsitem.headline: Blair tells Kohl to modernise for jobs and EMU.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair had some polite but firm advice for Europe's elder statesman, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, on Friday: Modernise your economy if you want to create jobs and make the euro work.
Fresh from warning Europe's centre-left parties at a congress in Sweden of the need to ditch outdated economic ideas, Blair wanted to deliver a similar message to Kohl.
Kohl, putting on a brave face despite a week of fending off fierce attacks on his government for economic and budgetary woes, had a warm welcome for Europe's youngest prime minister.
"We have dramatic changes to face in Europe and the world," he told Blair at his chancellery in Bonn.

Blair's advice on reforming the economy and labour markets was particularly poignant on a day Bonn took a new body blow in its battle to qualify for Europe's single currency with new figures showing another rise in unemployment.
To make sure his point came across to German voters, Blair said the same thing in a front-page commentary in the country's most popular newspaper, the mass-circulation Bild daily.

Speaking to reporters during his flight from a European socialist party meeting in Malmo in southern Sweden, Blair said: "In order to make the single market work and certainly if Europe proceeds towards a single currency, you have got to have the economies in proper shape.

"That means flexible labour makets, investment in education and skills and ensuring that we're developing the type of welfare state that is compatible with what is a completely different set of economic conditions today."

Aides said Blair won strong support for his ideas during bilateral meetings in Malmo with the prime ministers of Sweden and Denmark but was under no illusion that it would take time to convince Germany of the need to reform.

Commentators in Germany sometimes say Blair is to the right of Kohl, whose Christian Democratic Union (CDU) supports a "social market economy" with elements of intervention that look more like traditional social democratic policy than New Labour.

"I think we are building support for a genuine new third way in Europe, which means the role of government is not old-style state intervention or heaping regulations on employers -- but neither is it the way of conservative parties of simply letting people sink or swim in the market place," Blair said.

Asked whether the single currency risked becoming a potentially disastrous irrelevance, Blair -- who says it is highly unlikely Britain will join monetary union at the start -- said it was up to Germany to decide whether it wanted to press ahead with the project.
"If the single currency is fudged or the criteria for it are fiddled, or we don't take the measures of reform that we are suggesting in Europe... then there will be problems."

Germany's domestic debate about European economic and monetary union (EMU), long stifled by a broad consensus among the political elite, heated up this week after the Bundesbank forced Bonn to back down on its plans to revalue its assets.
Bonn had hoped the plan would help Germany fulfil EMU entry criteria.
Blair told Kohl he would work hard for an agreement at this month's European Union reform summit in Amsterdam.
"It is important that we get a successful conclusion at the Intergovernmental Conference in Amsterdam and we will work very hard on that," Blair said.
British officials said the biggest obstacle to be overcome at the summit was obtaining solid assurances that Britain would be able to retain control over its external borders.
